Field studies of the Lumptail searobin Prionotus stephanophrys along the southern Brazilian coast have provided detailed insights into its early life history. At a stable water temperature of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], the embryonic period is quite brief, with eggs hatching after just 9 days [ab = 9 days] of incubation. The resulting yolk-sac larvae are diminutive, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams]. This initial mass, reflecting the small egg diameter typical of the genus, places the species among the smaller-bodied triglids at the moment of chorion rupture. The rapid pace of early embryogenesis is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy, allowing larvae to enter the planktonic environment quickly and exploit ephemeral prey patches. Following hatching, the larvae initiate exogenous feeding shortly after yolk-sac resorption, a critical transition that marks the onset of the pelagic larval phase.

As the juveniles grow and approach the transition to benthic life, a key developmental threshold is reached when individuals attain a total length at puberty of 22.6 centimeters [Lp = 22.6 centimeters]. This length, corresponding to the onset of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, marks the beginning of reproductive capacity. At this size, a typical female searobin has a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 114.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 114.3 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue necessary to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis. The length-mass relationship, derived from an extensive morphometric dataset, indicates a strong allometric scaling of body mass with total length. Individuals at this pubertal stage have already undergone the allometric shift associated with metamorphosis and have taken up a demersal existence on sandy substrates, where they forage on benthic crustaceans.

The maximum size attainable by this species, as documented from the largest specimens captured in trawl surveys off the coast of São Paulo, is an ultimate total length of 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters]. At this terminal size, females reach their ultimate female wet weight of 767.5 grams [Wwi = 767.5 grams], a substantial body mass that positions the Lumptail searobin as a moderately large member of its genus, comparable in mass to other demersal triglids that forage on continental shelves. This asymptotic body size is achieved after a prolonged period of somatic growth, with individuals continuing to add mass slowly well after the onset of sexual maturity. The growth trajectory, which follows a decelerating curve typical of teleosts with indeterminate growth, suggests that resources in later life are increasingly partitioned toward reproductive output rather than further increases in length. Such a pattern is common among demersal triglids that inhabit continental shelf environments.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated from gravid females captured during the spawning season. At the prevailing water temperature of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is realized through a combination of batch spawnings. Field observations indicate that a single female produces approximately 274 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 274 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning period, a rate that reflects both the number of oocytes ovulated per batch and the frequency of spawning events. This daily fecundity was calculated by extrapolating from the batch fecundity of the closely related congener Prionotus evolans for a female of equivalent total length, adjusted for the thermal regime of the collection site. The sustained high output over several weeks suggests a strategy of capitalizing on warm, productive coastal waters.

Longevity estimates for Prionotus stephanophrys, derived from recaptures of tagged individuals and validated by otolith annulus counts, indicate a lifespan of up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] at a temperature of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, recorded for fish maintained at the same thermal conditions of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], places the species among the longer-lived members of the family Triglidae. Such a life span, combined with early maturation at a modest body size, implies a life-history strategy that balances relatively high annual adult survivorship with a protracted reproductive window. The oldest individuals examined showed signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced gonadosomatic indices and lower batch fecundities. This pattern of gradual physiological decline in very old age is consistent with the slow pace of life typical of demersal fishes in stable, subtropical shelf environments.
